project.name: mockx
project.description: MockX is a deterministic FIX-speaking mock exchange for strategy testing and simulation, combining an exact price-time order book and controlled clock with REST administration, immutable WebSocket market data, optional QuestDB persistence, and experimental ITCH/GLIMPSE feeds. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Exchange Purpose and Contracts
tour.description: Start with the README to establish what MockX simulates and which public interfaces it supports. FIX carries order entry, REST controls simulation administration, and WebSocket plus optional native feeds expose committed market data. Keep the documented matching, timing, ownership and immutable-report guarantees in view as you follow the implementation.

tour.title: Exact Values and State
tour.description: The shared models define the commands, mutable orders, FIFO books and immutable reports used throughout the exchange. Numeric helpers and instrument metadata translate decimal wire values into exact integer ticks and lots, then format results without changing authoritative quantities. These files supply the vocabulary and accounting rules needed to understand every later subsystem.
tour.languageLesson: Python dataclasses can represent both mutable aggregates and frozen snapshots. Follow which object owns mutation: an immutable report must capture scalar values rather than retain a live mutable order.

tour.title: Configuration and Process Ownership
tour.description: With the domain types established, follow a concrete local configuration through strict validation and the CLI into MockExchange. The composition root owns the engine, scheduler, gateway, API, metrics and native feeds, including their startup, readiness and shutdown. Reading these files together shows where runtime policy is selected and where component references are wired.
tour.languageLesson: Pydantic models turn configuration data into typed objects and enforce relationships between settings. The configuration file shows user-facing values; the model definitions explain which combinations are accepted.

tour.title: Price-Time Matching
tour.description: The matching engine applies the command and quantity rules introduced earlier to authoritative order books. Follow submission through price/FIFO matching, participant self-cross prevention and the treatment of market or IOC remainders. Cancellation and native replacement share this state, while each completed action produces immutable execution reports and committed displayed-order events.

tour.title: Deterministic Simulated Time
tour.description: The scheduler determines when engine commands and delivery events run, so simulated latency becomes part of reproducible exchange behavior. Equal timestamps retain FIFO order, advancement includes events exactly at the target, and a failed generation retains dead-letter diagnostics. Real monotonic CPU durations remain separate from the simulated timestamps used by the business workflow.
tour.languageLesson: An async handler can suspend while the scheduler awaits it; async execution alone does not define event ordering. The explicit queue order and advancement loop establish the simulator's timing guarantees.

tour.title: Atomic Session Boundaries
tour.description: Session lifecycle control coordinates the engine and scheduler as one simulation generation. It serializes start/end transitions, administrative advancement, ingress and snapshot capture so consumers observe stable boundaries. Accepted transitions are protected from cancellation, and metric loss can fail a run at a command boundary rather than leave ambiguous progress.

tour.title: FIX Ingress and Delivery
tour.description: Now follow the public order-entry path from QuickFIX callbacks into generation-qualified, ordered commands. Stable session ownership and ClOrdID claims keep routing and duplicate handling tied to the correct participant context. The retained delivery queue carries immutable logical responses through per-session FIFO ordering, versioned deadlines and bounded retry cycles.

tour.title: Administration and WebSocket Data
tour.description: The API exposes the lifecycle controls and committed state developed in the previous steps through typed REST, readiness, metrics and browser routes. WebSocket connections receive globally sequenced snapshots through bounded per-client buffers. Dedicated sender tasks and snapshot conflation isolate slow consumers while preserving the initial snapshot and error/close ordering.
tour.languageLesson: A dedicated asyncio sender task serializes writes for each client. Bounded queues make backpressure explicit, and conflation can replace obsolete snapshots while preserving protocol-critical frames.

tour.title: Native ITCH Publication
tour.description: The same committed displayed-order events can drive the optional downstream ITCH feed. The publisher owns run-scoped announcements and heartbeats, the encoder validates binary field representations, and the MoldUDP64 transport packs bounded multicast datagrams. Message-count sequencing connects these layers and gives downstream consumers a continuity boundary to track.
tour.languageLesson: Binary protocols require explicit byte widths, byte order and numeric bounds. Exact internal integers still need protocol-specific conversion, such as ITCH's implied-decimal Price(4) representation.

tour.title: Recovering a Feed Snapshot
tour.description: GLIMPSE complements live multicast with an authenticated snapshot recovery service over SoupBinTCP. Its listener outlives individual runs, while cached snapshot sessions and interrupted-spin replay remain bounded and generation-scoped. Trace the framed login, data and heartbeat controls to see how a client obtains a stable recovery cut before continuing with the live feed.

tour.title: Metrics and Persistence
tour.description: Metrics observe the matching, timing and delivery boundaries introduced so far, keeping event-owned counters and exact trade totals. Each persisted logical event has an immutable identity, and a bounded writer manages asynchronous admission, retries and final draining. The QuestDB adapter requires acknowledged writes and fixed WAL schemas so timestamp collisions and retries do not erase distinct events.

tour.title: Historical Market Replay
tour.description: The replay example puts the exchange contracts to work with historical CoinAPI order-book data. Source parsing preserves exact ticks, lots, nanosecond timestamps and order lifetimes without exposing future state. The runner then coordinates paced releases, FIX acknowledgements and observed market data, producing quality and timing results for the completed replay.

tour.title: Native Consumers and Routing
tour.description: The C++ examples exercise the native feed from the consumer side of the exchange boundary. The feed handler combines a bounded multicast ring with GLIMPSE recovery and sequence stitching, then publishes reconstructed depth. The smart order router uses ready venue depth to plan price-prioritized sweeps with parent limits, exact lot quantities and deterministic venue tie-breaking.

tour.title: Proving the Invariants
tour.description: Return to the core guarantees with tests that deliberately corrupt cached book state and generate long command histories. The invariant suite checks independent consistency properties rather than relying only on example outcomes. Generated replacement histories extend those checks across revisions and displayed liquidity, connecting the engine behavior to the feed contracts.

tour.title: Running the Complete System
tour.description: Finish by connecting the components to a runnable demonstration. The Docker image packages Python, native QuickFIX dependencies, the application and its protocol assets, while Compose brings together QuestDB, MockX, the multicast relay and the continuous FIX driver. Health dependencies gate traffic until the required services are ready, making the startup ownership from Step 3 concrete.
